extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature and theatre; playwrights, comic writers, and theorists of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical theory of the comic: identifies fundamental processes (repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference) in events and language that produce laughter, with guidance and examples for recognising or producing comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisation of life as the comic objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy aims to obtain a MECHANISATION of life: to treat life as if it were a repeating mechanism with reversible action and interchangeable parts, thereby producing a ludicrous effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life is ordinarily evolution in time and complexity in space (continuous change, irreversibility, individuality). Comedy contrasts with this by introducing mechanism into forms of life. The comic objective is to present actions/relations as mechanically repeatable, reversible or interchangeable—an artificial exaggeration of natural rigidity. This is the unifying aim behind the other methods (repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition (method of light comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation (combination of circumstances) recurs several times in its original form and thus contrasts with the changing stream of life; repetition produces comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetitions are more laughable the more complex and naturally introduced the repeated scene is—two conditions a playwright must reconcile. Forms include repeating same arrangement of events through a play (e.g., Moliere's plays: Ecole des femmes, George Dandin) or reproducing a scene with different character groups (masters then servants). Contemporary comedy often prepares the audience's mind to accept coincidence; classical comedy makes repetition seem natural by character constancy. Anti-pattern: flat, obviously contrived repetition that lacks believable introduction or complexity will fail to amuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (method of comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverse the situation or invert roles (subject↔object) so that the outcome recoils on the author or original role is turned upside down; the role-reversal itself produces humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a prisoner lecturing the magistrate, a child teaching parents, the villain being victim of his own villainy ('robber robbed'). The inverted scene need not be shown; a mental image suffices. Inversion is closely related to repetition and is the least interesting of the three linguistic/situational laws but easy to apply (e.g., reversing grammatical roles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of series (equivocal situations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation is comic when it belongs simultaneously to two independent series of events and can be interpreted in two entirely different meanings at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage-made misunderstandings are a particular case: each character follows his own series and interprets events correctly relative to that series, but the partial coincidence of the series creates equivocal situations. Laughter arises because the audience perceives both independent series and their precarious reconciliation; the author must continually remind us of their independence and coincidence. Variants include interference between past and present series, mock-heroic transpositions, and nested 'comedy within a comedy.' Anti-pattern: failing to sustain awareness of the two independent series will collapse the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absentmindedness/rigidity as source of the ludicrous
rubrics_metrics.description: The ludicrous in events is absentmindedness in things; the ludicrous in character results from some fundamental absentmindedness in the person. Rigidity and automatism provoke laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because life is normally continuous and alert, any lapse (rigidity, stereotyped formula, mechanical action) stands out as comic. Light comedy exaggerates such absentmindedness (like a jointed dancing-doll), converting slight natural lapses into an art that pleases because laughter is pleasurable. Anti-pattern: treating absentmindedness as merely a fault to be corrected; in comedy it must be signalled and often amplified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: comic expressed vs comic created by language
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a distinction between comic EXPRESSED (which could be translated) and comic CREATED BY LANGUAGE (which owes its effect to sentence structure or word choice and generally cannot be translated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic expressed can survive translation though some nuance may be lost; comic created by language depends on language-specific structures (phonetics, idioms, gender, set phrases). For producing or evaluating linguistic jokes, determine whether the humor stems from content that transfers across languages or from language-specific forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witty (esprit) versus comic — target of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: A word is comic when it makes us laugh at the person who utters it, and witty when it makes us laugh at a third party or at ourselves; wit is the comic in a volatile state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broader sense: wit is a 'dramatic way of thinking' that sets ideas conversing as if on stage. Restricted sense relevant to comedy: the knack for dashing off delicate comic scenes (‘dashing them off so subtly that all is over as soon as we notice them’). For crafting wit, aim for a compact verbal scene that projects to a larger comic situation. Note: many utterances are ambiguous between witty and comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for analyzing or producing wit: expand remark into a comic scene
rubrics_metrics.description: To analyse a witty remark, enlarge it into a regular scene and then identify the category of the comic to which the scene belongs; this reveals the comic structure underlying the witticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: take a concise witty saying, imagine the extended scene it implies, classify it (repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference, etc.). This both explains and helps craft wit: produce a mini-scene that fits a known comic mechanism. Example: Mme. de Sevigne's 'Your chest hurts me' expanded into Moliere's Amour Medecin scenario.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic-by-absurdity-in-a-formula: absurd idea in a ready-made phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: A COMIC MEANING IS INVARIABLY OBTAINED WHEN AN ABSURD IDEA IS FITTED INTO A WELL-ESTABLISHED PHRASE-FORM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stereotyped phrase-forms lull attention; inserting an absurdity reveals automatisms and produces laughter. Example: 'Ce sabre est le plus beau jour de ma vie' — absurd idea grafted on a familiar phrase ending. For writing humor, identify stock phrase-forms and introduce a clear absurdity to mark automatism. Anti-pattern: obscuring the phrase-form so the automatism isn't perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literalising a figurative expression (materialising metaphors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic effect arises whenever we pretend to take literally an expression which was used figuratively; fixing attention on the material/physical aspect of a metaphor makes it comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: interpreting 'Tous les arts sont freres' in a physical family sense, or converting metaphorical verbs into concrete actions to create a visual joke. To craft such comic lines, choose metaphors with vivid concrete imagery and force a literal reading. Anti-pattern: picking metaphors too abstract to yield a concrete image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical vs moral meaning shift in language
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh if our attention is diverted to the physical in a person when it is the moral that is in question; many words have both a physical and a moral meaning and comic arises from emphasising the physical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit words with concrete origins whose figurative sense is expected; by foregrounding the physical sense one produces a comic image. Example rejoinders that force a bodily, sporting, or material reading of a figurative phrase to trap the speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic transformation of sentences: three linguistic laws (inversion, reciprocal interference, transposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences become comic by (1) inversion (reverse grammatical roles or meanings), (2) reciprocal interference of two sets of ideas (puns, double meanings, play upon words), and (3) transposition (putting ideas into an alien style or key, analogous to repetition in action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative importance: inversion is least interesting but easy; reciprocal interference (puns → play upon words) is an inexhaustible source; transposition is most far-reaching (equivalent to repetition for events) and involves placing ideas in a different stylistic environment while preserving relations. Examples: grammatical reversals, puns (phonetic homophones), play upon words using multiple meanings of the same sentence, and translating a thought into an incongruous stylistic key. For creating verbal comedy, prefer transposition and true play upon words over cheap homophonic puns; ensure the transposed style still preserves semantic relations to produce the comic contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play upon words vs pun: genuine semantic interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate the pun (two different sentences that sound alike) from a true play upon words (one sentence that genuinely expresses two independent sets of ideas). The play upon words indicates a lapse of attention in language and is more subtle than a mere pun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer constructions where a single written/uttered sentence can plausibly carry two meanings (especially by exploiting figurative vs literal senses) rather than relying solely on phonetic coincidence. The play upon words is closer to metaphor and can be philosophically illuminating; it also betrays negligence/lapse in language which is part of its comic value. Anti-pattern: relying exclusively on homophonic puns that do not produce genuine double interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition as linguistic repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposition is to ordinary language what repetition is to comedy: transferring an arrangement of ideas into a fresh stylistic environment (another 'key') while keeping their mutual relations yields comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You need not show both the original and transposed expressions; suggesting the incongruous setting or style can suffice. This device is powerful for producing comic distance and highlighting mechanisation of thought. Example guidance: take thoughts naturally expressed in one register and render them in an incongruous register (e.g., solemn diction applied to trivial subject).
